insider_note: Adding and subtracting eˣ in the numerator turns an awkward-looking fraction into a plain 1 minus a f′/f form — no substitution is even needed once this rewriting is done.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Write the integrand as 1 minus a fraction
steps.why: Adding and subtracting eˣ in the numerator splits the fraction into a plain 1 and an f′(x)/f(x) form for f(x)=1+eˣ, since d/dx(1+eˣ)=eˣ exactly.
common_mistakes: Trying a substitution t=eˣ first instead of the simpler direct rewriting, which also works but takes longer.
Splitting 1/(1+eˣ) as 1 − 1/(1+eˣ), which is not a valid algebraic step.
steps.memory_tip: Add and subtract eˣ in the numerator to expose the f′/f shape hiding inside 1/(1+eˣ).

steps.label: Integrate for the final answer
steps.why: ∫1 dx = x and ∫eˣ/(1+eˣ) dx = log(1+eˣ) (an f′/f form, no modulus needed since 1+eˣ is always positive), subtracted as the split in step 1 requires.
common_mistakes: Adding the modulus bars on log(1+eˣ) unnecessarily — 1+eˣ is always positive, so |1+eˣ|=1+eˣ, but writing the bars is not wrong, just not required here.
Sign slip, writing x + log(1+eˣ) instead of x − log(1+eˣ).
steps.memory_tip: 1+eˣ is ALWAYS positive (eˣ>0 for every x), so this is the one log in the chapter that genuinely needs no modulus bars.
